title: Comparing the Classic Sorts & the Ω(n log n) Lower Bound
summary: Merge sort, quicksort, and heapsort all cost O(n log n) — the real choice comes down to stability, memory, and cache behavior, and why no comparison sort can beat n log n at all.

slides.markdown:
[merge-sort](merge-sort), [quicksort-partitioning](quicksort-partitioning), and heapsort all carry the same headline complexity: O(n log n). If Big-O were the whole story, it wouldn't matter which one you picked. It does matter, and the reasons are exactly the things Big-O deliberately throws away: **stability**, **memory footprint**, and **cache behavior**.

This topic is the decision framework — when each one actually wins — plus the theoretical floor underneath all three: no algorithm that sorts by comparing elements can beat **Ω(n log n)**, ever, which is why every one of these sorts converges on the same exponent instead of one of them finding something better.

slides.sectionTitle: Stability: why merge sort preserves equal-key order and quicksort/heapsort don't
slides.markdown:
Merge sort is stable because its merge step has an explicit, controllable tie-break: when two elements are equal, always take from the left half first, and the left half's elements always originated earlier. That's a one-line guarantee you can point to in the code.

Quicksort and heapsort have no equivalent hook. Quicksort's partitioning swaps elements based on comparisons to the pivot with no memory of original position — an equal-to-pivot element can end up on either side and in either order relative to another equal element. Heapsort's heapify operations move elements based on heap-order comparisons that are similarly blind to original position.

Both *can* be made stable by attaching the original index as a tiebreaker to every comparison, but that costs extra memory and comparisons, defeating the reason you picked an in-place sort in the first place — so in practice, if stability matters, you reach for merge sort rather than patch quicksort or heapsort.

slides.sectionTitle: In-place vs extra memory: O(1)/O(log n) space for quicksort/heapsort vs O(n) for merge sort
slides.markdown:
Heapsort is the cleanest of the three on memory: it builds the heap **inside the input array** and needs no auxiliary storage at all beyond a few loop variables — true **O(1)** extra space, no recursion required if implemented iteratively.

Quicksort is in-place in the same sense — no second array — but pays for its recursive calls with a stack that costs **O(log n)** with good pivot discipline (recurse into the smaller half first), or O(n) in the worst case without that discipline.

Merge sort needs a genuine second buffer to merge into, costing **O(n)** auxiliary space at its peak (reused across levels, but the peak doesn't shrink), plus O(log n) recursion stack.

When memory is the binding constraint — sorting close to the limit of available RAM, or a memory-constrained device — heapsort's O(1) guarantee is the strongest of the three, which is precisely its real niche despite rarely being the default choice otherwise (slide 9).

The pattern worth internalizing from this chart: merge sort and heapsort both have **no bad case** — their worst case matches their best case, because neither one's split point (merge sort's midpoint, heapsort's heap-order comparisons) depends on data shape. Quicksort is the only one of the three with a genuine gap between average and worst case, because its split point depends on the pivot and the data.

slides.sectionTitle: Merge sort vs quicksort vs heapsort — stability, space, cache behavior, worst case
slides.markdown:
| | Merge sort | Quicksort | Heapsort |
|---|---|---|
| Stable | Yes | No | No |
| Extra space | O(n) | O(log n) (stack) | O(1) |
| Worst case | O(n log n) | O(n²) (rare, randomized) | O(n log n) |
| Cache behavior | Sequential, good | Sequential within partition, good | Poor — jumps across the heap array |
| Typical real-world speed | Good | Usually fastest | Usually slowest of the three |
| Best used when | Stability required, linked lists, external sort | Default in-memory choice | Hard memory or worst-case guarantee needed |

No single row wins across the board — this table is the whole point of the topic. An interviewer asking "which sort would you use" is really asking whether you can map a constraint (stability? memory? worst-case risk?) to the row that satisfies it.

slides.sectionTitle: Why comparison sorting can't beat Ω(n log n) — the decision-tree argument
slides.markdown:
Any sorting algorithm that only learns about the data by comparing pairs of elements can be modeled as a **decision tree**: each internal node is one comparison, each leaf is one possible final ordering (permutation) of the input. For the algorithm to be correct, every one of the n! possible orderings of n distinct elements must correspond to at least one leaf.

A binary tree with n! leaves needs depth at least **log₂(n!)**, since a tree of depth d has at most 2^d leaves. By Stirling's approximation, log₂(n!) is Θ(n log n).

The number of comparisons an algorithm makes on its worst-case input is at least the tree's depth — so **every comparison-based sort needs Ω(n log n) comparisons in the worst case**, full stop. This is why merge sort, quicksort, and heapsort all land on the same exponent: none of them are settling for a good-enough bound, they're all hitting a mathematical floor that no comparison-based algorithm can get under.

slides.sectionTitle: Cache behavior and constant factors: why quicksort usually beats merge sort in practice
slides.markdown:
Both sorts are Θ(n log n), yet quicksort routinely runs faster on real hardware. The reasons live entirely below the Big-O line.

Quicksort's partitioning scans and swaps within a **contiguous** subarray in place — sequential memory access the CPU's prefetcher handles well, and no allocation. Merge sort's merge step reads from two separate halves and writes into a **separate buffer**, which touches more distinct memory regions and pays allocation cost for every level of temporary buffers (even when reused, there's bookkeeping overhead absent from quicksort's plain index arithmetic).

Quicksort also tends to do fewer total element moves in the common case, since Hoare-style partitioning only swaps elements confirmed to be misplaced, while merge sort's merge unconditionally copies every element at every level.

None of this shows up in Big-O, which is exactly why "they're both O(n log n)" is an incomplete answer to "which is faster" — the honest answer names the constant-factor and cache reasons underneath the shared exponent.

slides.sectionTitle: What production languages actually run — Python/Java's Timsort vs C++'s introsort
slides.markdown:
No mainstream language ships a textbook-pure version of any one of these three sorts — production sorts are hybrids built to dodge each one's individual weakness.

**Timsort** (Python's `sorted()`/`list.sort()`, Java's `Arrays.sort()` for objects) is a merge-sort derivative that first scans for naturally occurring sorted "runs" in the real data, extends short runs with insertion sort, then merges runs with a size-balancing rule that keeps the merges efficient. It's stable — required, since both languages sort objects by arbitrary comparators where callers expect stability — and it's dramatically faster than plain merge sort on partially-sorted real-world data.

**Introsort** (C++'s `std::sort`) starts as quicksort for its cache-friendly speed, but **monitors recursion depth** and switches to heapsort if the depth exceeds roughly 2·log₂(n) — converting quicksort's rare O(n²) risk into a guaranteed O(n log n) worst case — then switches to insertion sort for small subarrays (typically under ~16 elements) where its low constant factor wins outright.

Both hybrids exist because no single classic sort is unconditionally best; production code picks the strategy per situation instead of committing to one algorithm's trade-offs everywhere.

slides.sectionTitle: Heapsort's real niche: in-place and worst-case-safe, rarely the practical default
slides.markdown:
Heapsort (see the heaps group for the underlying structure) builds a max-heap from the array in place, then repeatedly swaps the max to the end and re-heapifies the shrinking prefix — genuinely O(1) extra space and a guaranteed O(n log n) worst case, with no data-dependent bad case at all.

So why isn't it the default? Its access pattern jumps across the array by heap-index arithmetic (parent at `i`, children at `2i+1` and `2i+2`), which scatters memory accesses far more than quicksort's contiguous partitioning or merge sort's sequential merge — poor cache locality translates directly into a larger real-world constant factor despite the identical Big-O.

Its genuine niche is exactly where quicksort's O(n²) risk and merge sort's O(n) space are both unacceptable at once: hard real-time systems that cannot tolerate a slow tail, or memory-constrained embedded contexts. Introsort (previous slide) captures heapsort's worst-case safety as a *fallback*, which is the more common way heapsort shows up in practice — as a guarantee lurking behind quicksort, not as the primary algorithm.

slides.sectionTitle: Picking a sort by Big-O alone and ignoring its stability guarantee
slides.markdown:
"They're all O(n log n), so it doesn't matter" is the single most common wrong answer to "which sort would you use." It ignores the property that most often actually determines correctness in real code: **stability**.

Concrete failure: sort a list of transactions by amount, then need them still grouped by original timestamp order within each amount tier — swap in an unstable in-place sort for a "faster" alternative and that secondary ordering silently scrambles, with no error, no crash, just wrong grouping that might not even be noticed until a report looks off.

The question to ask before picking a sort by complexity alone: **does this data get sorted more than once, by different keys, where the earlier order needs to survive?** If yes, stability isn't optional, and quicksort or heapsort are disqualified regardless of their speed advantage — no amount of "it's faster" fixes a data-correctness bug.

slides.sectionTitle: Assuming "in-place" means zero extra memory anywhere, including the call stack
slides.markdown:
"In-place" describes the data — no second copy of the array — not the total memory footprint of the running algorithm. A recursive in-place quicksort still needs a call stack, and without the discipline of recursing into the smaller partition first, that stack can grow to **O(n)** on an unbalanced split, quietly defeating the memory benefit the label implied.

The same gap applies whenever "O(1) space" is claimed for a recursive algorithm generally: recursion depth is memory, full stop, whether or not you allocated an explicit array. Heapsort's genuine O(1) claim holds specifically because a typical implementation is a **loop**, not recursion — that's the actual reason it's the tightest of the three on memory, not just that it avoids a second array.

When a memory budget is the real constraint — not just "avoid allocating a second array" but "bound total memory including the stack" — verify the implementation is iterative or has a provable log-depth recursion bound, not just that it swaps elements in place.
